To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the new prescription guidelines are applied more widely in settlements with higher average income, the adoption of new prescription guidelines is spatially concentrated, the use of antibiotics among young children increased in response to the price subsidy.
the application of the policy is spatially clustered, it is more widespread in richer settlements, and it increases the use of antibiotics among the target group.
the implementation of new prescription guidelines is spatially selective and the reduced user fees for antibiotics among children under age 5 increased their consumption.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the implementation of the new prescription guideline and its effect on antibiotic use.
the implementation of the new prescription policy and the effect of reduced user fees for antibiotics on antibiotic use.
the spatial variation in prescription practices, and the effects of the reduced user fees on antibiotic use.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the new prescription guidelines have been implemented selectively, with a positive effect on the use, but with the potential of increasing the imbalance between the use of antibiotics in different socioeconomic groups.
the new guidelines were not implemented in a way that could achieve their goals.
the policy is not fully effective and the effect of the reduced co-payments for children aged 0–4 on their antibiotic use is small.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the policy of reducing user fees for antibiotics in Hungary was not implemented in a way that would have been expected, and it did not lead to the intended reduction in the antibiotic use.
the new prescription guidelines are not effective in reducing the out-of-pocket expenses of antibiotics among poor children.
a price subsidy of antibiotics may lead to a higher consumption of antibiotics, but the effect is smaller than expected.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of price subsidies on antibiotic use may not be uniform across different groups of users.
policies aimed at improving access to medicines need to take into account the heterogeneity in implementation and the spatial clustering of the effects of such policies.
the effect of the price subsidy on antibiotic use can only be understood if the spatial variation in implementation is taken into account.
